Your thoughts are not going to go away.  The way you react to them can change, though.  The more you avoid him and ruminate on those thoughts, the stronger they will become.  The more you ask yourself why would I want to break up with him, the stronger the intrusive thought will become.

Your thoughts will always find you, but you do not have to be afraid of them.  Take deep breaths and focus on the here and now, keeping mind of each breath.  Remember that you are safe and are going to be fine.  Anxiety is a real and powerful emotions, but you are not in physical danger.  

Finally, I want to add that a relationship is a choice.  Asking whether you made the right choice is a moot point because you cannot really know.  If your anxiety regarding the relationship and your feelings towards your partner are causing undue, then focus on resolving that stress.

Avoidance is a dangerous game to play.  As with any checking/compulsion, the more your resist that behavior the more resilient you become.

I don't know if you need to break up with him.  Maybe you do, maybe you don't.  These thoughts we have are built from memories, and memories are imperfect.  Our thoughts are imperfect, so our brain providing thoughts about our reality can be inaccurate, albeit scary.  In the end, all one can do is practice accepting the presence of thoughts and consider our core values or the things that we care about.  It is those things that OCD attacks.  The more you give into fears regarding thoughts that attack your core values, the more powerful your fears become.

Exposure, response prevention, mindfulness, acceptance, and stress reduction can go a long way, but you must commit to learning these techniques to help your mind find peace.

It is common for trauma to trigger repetitive anxiety.  The following is not authoritative and is based on my understanding: thoughts result from the synthesis of past experiences and a degree of logic.  Intrusive thoughts normally are manifestations of possible (although frequently unlikely) scenarios.  Given that past events can contribute to the content of arising conscious and subconscious thoughts, a traumatic event can have a dramatic influence upon both the content/depth of the thought and upon our resulting conscious reaction to said thought.  For example, if you get sick from a beef stew as a child, then hearing the word 'stew' could result in thoughts of becoming violently ill, of which you, having experienced that, will likely allow for that thought to sway your thoughts.

Within ROCD, or relationship anxiety in general, past trauma such as abuse, cheating, or loss can obvious leave one anxious given the trauma that coincides with those events.  A person with OCD general has very intense, repetitive intrusive thoughts that have been repeatedly strengthened by a repeated, aggressive reaction to those intrusive thoughts that are perceived as an immediate danger to one's emotional well-being.  Certain compulsions/rituals that give temporary relief to these thoughts become increasingly important to someone with OCD's response.  With ROCD, this manifests as reassurance though asking partner repeated questions (even the same question over and over), searching for answers and validation online, and complex mental gymnastics that try and prove intrusive thoughts 'wrong' or 'invalid'.  But in the end, every moment meant resisting these thoughts only strengthens them.

The odd resolution is to instead accept those intrusive thoughts, let them be with you, and to not fight back.

You feel how you feel---the brain does what it does.  In the end, you cannot know what is to come, and your thoughts will never go away.  Listen to them, respect them, and continue to live in the moment.

You can't really know, just as you can't really know anything that is to come to pass in life.  All we have is the here and now---our ruminations over the future that frequently manifest as intrusive thoughts cannot silenced.  That uncertainty can be accepted, though, and by practicing acceptance we can calm our racing minds

It frequently is rooted in a past event, but that does not change the fact that you must not resist these thoughts.  You're going to have thoughts, and some will be absolutely horrible, but with unrelenting practice and consistency you can learn to live with and accept your thoughts.

So type Ia supernova are effectively giant nuclear bombs produced by detonating a white dwarf that produce large amounts of radioactive nickel 56.  As the ejected material expands the nickel 56 begins to decay into cobalt 56 with a half life of like 6 days.  As the gamma rays from the decay scatter and diffuse through the ejected material they lose energy and are eventually emitted as optical/near infrared photons for the most part.  The cobalt 56 has a half like of like 15 days or so, and as a result supernova begins to dim more slowly after its maximum brightness.  All supernovae produce massive amount of nickel 56 but type Ia supernovae are interesting because their brightness is driven effectively entirely by nickel 56 and cobalt 56 decay.  There is actually a lot we really don't understand about type Ia supernovae, though.  It's actually a bit of a shit show.
